nameStory: Ocrepeira ectypa doesn't have a widely recognized common name, which isn't unusual for lesser-known orb weavers. The genus name Ocrepeira comes from Latin roots meaning 'swift' or 'quick,' possibly referring to their agile web-building behavior. With only three recorded observations in New England, this spider remains one of our region's most mysterious arachnids.
description: Ocrepeira ectypa is a small orb weaver spider that belongs to the same family as garden spiders and other classic web-builders. Like other orb weavers, it creates the familiar circular, spoke-and-spiral webs that glisten with dew on autumn mornings. This species is quite rare in New England, making any sighting a special discovery. Details about its exact size and appearance are limited due to its scarcity in scientific collections.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds a classic orb web with sticky spiral threads radiating from a central hub, typically spanning 6-12 inches across when fully constructed

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Typical orb weaver proportions with a rounded, bulbous abdomen and relatively slender legs that feel delicate if gently touched

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits at the center of its web or retreats to a silken hideaway at the web's edge when disturbed

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small to medium-sized orb weaver, with females typically larger than males as is common in this spider family

habitat: Given its rarity, specific habitat preferences in New England are not well documented. Like most orb weavers, it likely favors areas with suitable anchor points for web construction such as shrubs, forest edges, or gardens. The few recorded sightings suggest it may prefer more secluded woodland settings rather than open areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults may begin emerging and establishing territories, though specific timing is unclear due to limited observations.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most likely to be encountered, with spiders actively hunting and potentially mating.
seasonality.fall: Traditional peak season for orb weaver sightings, when females may be gravid and most conspicuous in their webs.
seasonality.winter: Likely overwinters as eggs or juveniles, with adults probably dying off after the first hard frosts.

funFact: This spider is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only three times in the region, making you more likely to see a bald eagle than encounter one of these elusive orb weavers!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small orb weavers in the genera Araneus or Neoscona, but the web structure and overall spider behavior would be very similar, making field identification challenging without expert examination.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England highlights how much we still don't know about our local spider fauna - there may be entire populations living quietly in habitats we haven't thoroughly surveyed yet.
compareHints: Since there are no other Ocrepeira species recorded in New England, comparisons must be made with other small orb weavers like Araneus species. The web construction and general body plan would be similar to other orb weavers, but specific distinguishing features require microscopic examination of reproductive structures. Its rarity alone sets it apart from more common orb weavers in our region.
